Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

for preposition

for the sake of, for a purpose

also for the sake of, for the good of, for fun, for doing, what for, sake, for my sake, for your sake, for reasons of health, for health reasons, for heaven’s sake

classical

Cato Agr. 157: valētūdinis causā experīrēs
Cic. Amic. 44: amīcōrum causā honesta faciāmus
Traupman 100: valētūdinis causā
Cic. Fam. 3.7.6: tuā causā (Lewis & Short s.v. labōrō)
Traupman 107: for the sake of; for your sake, causā (+ gen.); tuā (pl. vestrā) causā

causā + gen.

the ablative of causa, placed after its genitive

for the sake of; for (a purpose)

With a person’s pronoun, the possessive: meā causā, tuā causā, for my sake, for yours. With a gerund it gives the purpose: lūdendī causā, for play. See purpose.

Other words

  • grātiā + gen. — for the sake of, for

    the ablative of grātia, placed after its genitive · also used · classical · Gell. 5.14.21: quasi opis petendae grātiā; Quint. 1.1.26: irrītandae ad discendum īnfantiae grātiā

    Less common than causā in Cicero; at home in set phrases such as exemplī grātiā, for example.

  • ad + acc. — for (doing), for (an end)

    preposition with the accusative, often of a gerund or gerundive · also used · classical · Varr. RR 1.54.2: legitur ad bibendum, ēligitur ad edendum; Liv. 21.54.8: ope ūllā ad arcendum frīgus adhibitā

    What a thing is meant for: ad bibendum, for drinking.

  • cāsus datīvus — for (what a thing serves)

    construction: the dative, often of a gerundive · also used · classical · Mart. 14.144.1: tergendīs spongia mēnsīs ūtilis

    After ūtilis, aptus and in set phrases.

Examples

  • nūllus sūmptus est, et sī sūmptus esset, tamen valētūdinis causā experīrēs

    it costs nothing; and even if it did, you would still try it for your healthCato Agr. 157

  • haec igitur prīma lēx amīcitiae sanciātur, ut ab amīcīs honesta petāmus, amīcōrum causā honesta faciāmus

    let this be the first law of friendship: ask friends only for what is right, and do only what is right for friends’ sakeCic. Amic. 44

  • Salūtis causā bene fit hominī injūria.

    To hurt someone for the sake of his health is to do right.Publil. Sent. S 59

  • sublātum pedem ostendere mihi et porgere quasi opis petendae grātiā vīsus est

    he seemed to lift his paw, show it to me and hold it out, as if to ask for helpGell. 5.14.21

  • in vindēmiā dīligentis ūva nōn sōlum legitur sed etiam ēligitur; legitur ad bibendum, ēligitur ad edendum

    at a careful man’s vintage the grapes are not only picked but picked over: picked for drinking, picked over for eatingVarr. RR 1.54.2

  • haec tibi sorte datur tergendīs spongia mēnsīs ūtilis, expressō cum levis imbre tumet

    this sponge is your prize in the draw, useful for wiping tables when, squeezed dry, it swells up lightMart. 14.144.1–2

See also purpose, for, due to.
